newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia wood panel exports seen improving.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia wood panel exports seen improving.

text.p: Indonesian wood panel exports were promising due to a construction surge in Japan, while China's market had great potential, an industry executive said on Monday.

Tjipto Wignjoprajitno, executive director of the Indonesia Wood Panel Association (Apkindo), also said that there was no need for competition among top producers Indonesia, Malaysia and Brazil as supply was trailing demand.
"Construction in Japan is going up and panels are so (much) in demand," he told Reuters in an interview.
Headed by tycoon Muhammad Hasan, Apkindo has a monopoly on plywood exports and channels them through agents in Japan, China, South Korea and the Middle East.
Wignjoprajitno said 1996 wood panel exports were forecast at more than $4 billion, against $3.9 billion last year. The construction recovery in Japan would help maintain momentum.
"There will be an increase in last-quarter demand this year, especially from Japan," he said. "The economic recovery in Japan is beginning to bear fruit.
"The market looks promising," he said, adding that 1996 exports to Japan were expected to be around 3.23 million cubic metres (113 million cubic feet), up from 2.9 million last year.
Wignjoprajitno said China had huge potential as an export market, because of the housing needs of the world's most populated country.
"The potential is there. China has 1.2 billion people and it will need to build houses. But this will only happen when they have the money," he said.
Wignjoprajitno said a construction campaign in China would depend on trade with the United States. "More exports to the United States means more money and a pick up in demand," he said.
U.S. brokerage Merrill Lynch said in a report that China was expected to become a major plywood consumer in the second half of next year.

The official Antara news agency quoted the report as saying Chinese demand this year had been weak due to tight monetary controls and ample stocks, causing domestic plywood prices to fall to a low of $380 per cubic metre in January last year.
The report said that China's private sector consumption of plywood was likely to recover following the government's cutting of lending rates in August this year.
Wignjoprajitno said timber produced from land clearing was becoming a steady source of raw material for wood panels, adding that a cap on logging in natural forests would not hurt supply.
"Land clearing activities have produced 2.6 million cubic metres of timber of small diameters in the first five months of this year," he said. He did not have comparative data.
He said a government project to clear one million hectares (2.47 million acres) of land in Kalimantan was expected to keep supply steady over the next three to four years.
Wignjoprajitno said Indonesia had imposed some years ago a cap of 23.6 million cubic metres per year of timber from natural forests in a move aimed at sustaining the ecological balance.
He also said Indonesia was not competing with Malaysia and Brazil for market share as supply from all three could still not meet demand.
